course.title: AP United States History
course.description: A vertical-video APUSH course organized as units, chapters, lessons, and instructional scenes.
course.audience: APUSH students preparing for class assessments and the AP exam

presentation.visual_style: museum-documentary visuals with readable AP exam vocabulary

units.title: Period 1: Worlds Before and After Contact
units.description: Indigenous societies before European arrival, Atlantic exploration, the Columbian Exchange, and the first Spanish systems of conquest and labor.
learning_objectives: Explain how geography shaped diverse Indigenous societies before European contact.
Explain the causes and effects of European exploration in the Americas.
Evaluate how the Columbian Exchange transformed societies on both sides of the Atlantic.

chapters.title: Native Societies and Atlantic Contact
chapters.description: A three-lesson chapter moving from Indigenous regional diversity to the causes of European exploration and sustained Atlantic contact and exchange.
essential_questions: How did environment shape societies in North America before 1492?
Why did Atlantic contact produce unequal demographic, economic, and political consequences?
What combination of motives, ideas, and technology launched European exploration?
learning_objectives: Compare Indigenous societies in at least two North American regions.
Trace the motives and routes behind European exploration.
Use historical evidence to explain the effects of biological and commercial exchange.

lessons.title: North America Before European Contact
lessons.description: Regional diversity, environmental adaptation, exchange networks, and political organization before sustained European contact.
lessons.essential_question: How did geography and exchange shape diverse Indigenous societies before 1492?
learning_objectives: Identify how climate and available resources influenced settlement and subsistence.
Compare the social organization of societies in different regions.
Explain why North America in 1491 cannot be described as a single culture.

key_terms.definition: Cultivation of corn that supported population growth and settled communities.
A major Mississippian urban and ceremonial center near the Mississippi River.
Variation among societies produced by geography, resources, migration, and cultural choices.

narration.text: North America in 1491 was not one society waiting to be discovered. [beat] Millions of people lived in distinct communities, spoke many languages, and built economies adapted to local environments. The useful starting point is [emphasis]diversity[/emphasis], not a single stereotype.

narration.text: Near the Mississippi River, [awed] Cahokia became a large urban center supported by maize agriculture. Its monumental earthworks and far-reaching trade connections demonstrate [emphasis]organized labor[/emphasis], political authority, and exchange networks that linked communities across long distances.

Thin layered clouds move slowly across the sky; foreground grasses ripple in a light breeze; long sunlight and tree shadows shift gently over the mound and fields. The photographic composition stays fixed. Do not add buildings or people or text or modern objects.

narration.text: Different environments encouraged different strategies. [beat] Agricultural communities in the Southwest managed scarce water and built permanent settlements. On the Great Plains, many communities combined farming, hunting, and trade; later access to horses would change Plains life further. Environment influenced societies [emphasis]without mechanically determining them[/emphasis].

beats.text: What happens when the horse arrives?

[slow]Avoid treating Indigenous peoples as a single group or as passive actors.[/slow]

lessons.title: Atlantic Contact and the Columbian Exchange
lessons.description: European motives, transatlantic voyages, and the unequal consequences of biological and commercial exchange.
lessons.essential_question: Why did Atlantic contact transform Europe, Africa, and the Americas so unevenly?
learning_objectives: Explain the economic and political motives for European exploration.
Trace major categories of exchange across the Atlantic.
Evaluate why disease and coerced labor had especially destructive effects in the Americas.

key_terms.definition: The transfer of plants, animals, diseases, people, and ideas between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres after 1492.
A Spanish labor system granting colonists claims to Indigenous labor and tribute.
The interconnected system linking Europe, Africa, and the Americas through migration, trade, conquest, and slavery.

narration.text: By the late fifteenth century, European rulers sought new trade routes, wealth, and religious influence. [beat] Improvements in navigation and ship design made longer Atlantic voyages possible, while rivalry among states encouraged rulers to finance [emphasis]risky expeditions[/emphasis].

beats.text: Follow the route; then ask who financed it

narration.text: Ocean-going ships did more than move explorers. [awed] They connected ecosystems that had developed separately for thousands of years. [fast]Plants, animals, pathogens, people, and ideas[/fast] now traveled repeatedly in both directions across the Atlantic.

Every vessel, sail, and engraved detail stays in place. Do not add modern objects, text, or extra ships.
animation.caption: Sustained contact connected previously separate ecosystems

narration.text: The exchange created [emphasis]growth and catastrophe[/emphasis] at the same time. American crops such as maize and potatoes supported population growth elsewhere. Horses and other livestock changed labor and transportation in the Americas. [solemn][slow]But Afro-Eurasian diseases caused devastating Indigenous mortality, weakening communities[/slow] as Europeans expanded conquest and coerced labor.

Do not alter figures or add objects or romanticize coerced labor.

beats.text: Who gained power—and who paid the cost?

narration.text: The strongest explanation joins cause and consequence. [fast]Competition, commerce, and Christianity encouraged exploration; navigation made repeated crossings feasible;[/fast] biological exchange and coercive institutions then redistributed power and wealth unevenly. [beat] Contact created a connected Atlantic world, [emphasis]but not an equal one[/emphasis].

lessons.title: Why Europe Sailed West
lessons.description: Economic motives, crusading ideology, maritime technology, Columbus's miscalculation, and the papal division of the world — the causes of European exploration.
lessons.essential_question: Why did European rulers spend money on voyages into an unknown ocean?
learning_objectives: Explain the economic pressures that pushed Iberian rulers to seek a western route to Asia.
Describe how the Reconquista and new maritime technology made sustained Atlantic voyages possible.
Rank the motives of gold, God, and glory and justify the hierarchy with evidence.

key_terms.definition: The centuries-long Christian reconquest of Iberia from Muslim rule, completed with the fall of Granada in 1492.
A small, fast Portuguese sailing ship with lateen sails capable of sailing against the wind on long Atlantic voyages.
The 1494 papal agreement dividing newly discovered lands between Spain, west of the line, and Portugal, east of it.

narration.text: By the 1400s, Europe craved [emphasis]pepper, cinnamon, and silk[/emphasis]. And every bale crossed lands controlled by Ottoman and Italian middlemen who took a cut at each stop. Prices kept climbing before the goods reached Lisbon. [beat] A sea route straight to the spice islands would skip every taxman. And make its finder the richest merchant in Europe.

moves.label: Old route: taxed at every border

beats.text: Middlemen took a cut at every border
What made a shortcut worth the gamble?

narration.text: [fierce] Spain entered 1492 as a crusader state. After seven centuries of the Reconquista, Christian kingdoms retaking Iberia from Muslim rule, Granada fell, leaving an army with no enemy left to fight. [beat] The means came from Portugal: [emphasis]the caravel[/emphasis], a ship with lateen sails that could tack against winds, and [emphasis]the astrolabe[/emphasis], which fixed latitude from the stars. Technology made the gamble possible.

narration.text: Columbus was wrong. [beat] His math shrank the Earth's size to make Asia look reachable, and most experts correctly rejected it. But Ferdinand and Isabella had just united Spain, were flush with victory, and the price was tiny: [emphasis]three ships, one cast of the dice[/emphasis]. [pause:1] In 1494 a pope's treaty drew a line through the Atlantic. East of it Portugal's, west of it Spain's.

narration.text: Why did they sail? The answer comes in a triad: [fast]gold, God, and glory[/fast]. Gold meant spice profits and mines. It paid for everything. God meant converting souls and striking at Islam's flank. Glory meant crowns and a name on the map. [refrain]Be honest about the hierarchy: gold first.[/refrain] [beat] When they made landfall, they found a world on no map. Conquest comes next.

beats.text: What did they find across the ocean?
